items.title: Territorial Acknowledgement
notes: Councillor Freeman opened the meeting with the following Territorial Acknowledgement:

I would like to acknowledge that I was raised on the lands traditionally cared for by the Haudenosaunee, Lanape, and Anishinaabek peoples, covered by the Upper Canada Treaties. I was thankful to be accepted into Engineering at the University of Waterloo and move to the City where I have chosen to live and raise my family. These are the lands traditionally cared for by the Neutral, Anishinaabeg, and Haudenosaunee peoples, specifically within the Haldimand Tract, which is land granted to the Six Nations of the Grand River.

Earlier this month we celebrated International Women’s Day. As many of you know, engineering has shaped my life in many ways and is an amazing and meaningful career for women. As identified by Engineers Canada, Indigenous women are severely underrepresented in Canadian engineering, comprising only a small fraction of the profession. While initiatives exist to increase diversity, Indigenous women engineers face barriers including systemic discrimination, isolation, and underrepresentation.
Organizations like Engineers Canada and dedicated, trail-blazing professionals are working to improve access and representation.
In my land acknowledgement today, I would like to acknowledge the contribution to the engineering profession by the Indigenous community.

Mary Golda Ross was a Cherokee and American aerospace engineer. She was the first known Indigenous female engineer. She worked at Lockheed Corporation from 1942 until her retirement in 1973. She was one of the 40 founding engineers of the renowned and highly secretive Skunk Works project.

In 2018, Chelsea Banally became the first Indigenous woman to earn a PhD in engineering at the University of Alberta. Dr. Banally works on ways to treat tailing water, a toxic byproduct in the process of extracting bitumen from oil sands.
As a woman engineer, I would like to acknowledge the contributions made to the engineering profession from Indigenous engineering trailblazers like Mary Golda Ross and Dr. Chelsea Banally.

items.title: Moment of Reflection

At the beginning of this Council meeting, we pause to think about the needs of our community. May we show wisdom and compassion in all our decisions.

Wendy Fisher gave a presentation outlining the proposed development. She offered information on the background of the subject lands, the planning framework for the site, and conceptual plans for the proposal. Wendy Fisher then responded to questions of Council.

Dave Aston, Partner, MHBC Planning gave a presentation further detailed the proposed development, including renderings for the proposal, and additional background information. Dave Aston then responded to questions of Council.

items.title: Addendum: Funding Request – Immigration Waterloo
notes: Sanjay Govindaraj and Jim Bowman responded to questions of Council.
Tracey Hare, Immigration Waterloo Region and Tara Bedard, Immigration Waterloo Region also responded to questions of Council.
Councillor Roe having previously declared a pecuniary interest was absent for the taking of the vote.

Councillor Hanmer gave a shoutout to the University of Waterloo and the student committee that hosted the U Sports Women’s Ice Hockey Tournament in Elmira this past weekend, March 19-22. It was a fantastic weekend and everything moved smoothly.

Councillor Vasic wanted to highlight that the Button Factory Arts Centre is having a spring event in May, timing to be determined. It’s a reopening to celebrate some of the renovations they’ve done and what’s to come. There will be both paid and free events, as well as fundraising activities.

Councillor Wright mentioned that this past weekend on March 21, Conestoga College held their annual Pow Wow, which has been happening for 16 years. It was a fantastic event that was really well attended, with people from all across Canada.

Councillor Roe gave a shoutout to Team Dave at St. Davids for winning the Canadian Pacific First Robotics Competition in Vancouver a couple week ago. They are also competing this weekend at the University of Waterloo First Robotics Competition. They have an exceptional team, year after year, and it’s exciting to see how they all come together.
Councillor Freeman mentioned that Susan Aglukark, a Juno award-winning Inuit artist, is coming to the University of Waterloo on March 31. She just released a new book, “Kihiani: A Memoir of Healing”.
Mayor McCabe noted that Council for a Day submissions close on April 1, and for Grade 5 students to submit their ideas.
